paras: The lynching of Jim Toler was the killing of a Black man by a mob of more than 100 men at Alamo, near Helena in Montgomery County, Georgia, early on the morning of August 11, 1910. Toler was accused of entering the bedroom of two daughters of a planter while they slept; a posse found him in a field the next day, and he was tied to a tree and shot to death. A single dispatch from Helena carried the story to papers from Maine to New Mexico over the following week, while no Georgia or Black newspaper account and no report of an inquest or arrest was found.

According to the Helena dispatch, someone entered the room of two daughters of "a prominent planter of Montgomery county" on Tuesday night, August 9, while the girls were in bed asleep. The fuller version of the dispatch stated that one of the girls was awakened when the intruder raised the mosquito netting over the bed, and that her screams frightened him away. Neither the planter nor his daughters were named in any of the reports.

A search began at once, and on the afternoon of Wednesday, August 10, a posse came upon Toler "working in a corn field" and accused him of the crime. A later rewrite in the Bradford County Telegraph of Starke, Florida, said instead that he was found "pulling fodder on a nearby plantation" by "a posse of infuriated citizens." Every version stated that Toler confessed, but the claim appears only in the dispatch, which does not say who heard the confession or under what conditions.

Early the next morning he was tied to a tree and shot to death by a mob that the dispatch put at "over 100 men," after which "the mob then dispersed." The Associated Press version printed in the Pensacola Journal said that "about one hundred men" caught him and that "great excitement" in the area abated once it became known he had been caught and lynched. Most texts gave the hour as 1 a.m. on Thursday, but the Norwich Bulletin's copy said 11 o'clock in the morning and an Alexandria Gazette digest said the lynching took place Wednesday night.
The coverage reports no inquest, arrest, grand jury inquiry or trial, and no member of the posse or mob was named.

The story reached the white press as a short telegraphic item datelined Helena, Ga., August 11 or 12, in two main wordings. The fuller text, with the mosquito netting and the corn field, ran in the South in the Birmingham Age-Herald and on the front page of the Montgomery Advertiser, and later in South Carolina and Tennessee weeklies. A condensed text circulated in Western dailies such as the Salt Lake Tribune, the Los Angeles Herald and the Albuquerque Morning Journal, several of which placed Alamo "seventy-seven miles" from Helena rather than seven. Spellings of the victim's name varied, appearing as Toller in Maine, Tolera in Pensacola and Tolero in Ogden.

Most headlines stated the act plainly, such as "Negro Tied to Tree and Shot Dead by Mob" and "Tie Negro to Tree and Shoot Him to Death," while the Daily Kennebec Journal's subhead led with the confession: "Who Confesses to Entering Room of Georgia Planter's Daughters." Some Southern papers took a lighter tone: the Pensacola Journal's headline read "Mob Made Quick Work of Him," and South Carolina weeklies ran the story as "Promptly Lyncher Him" with the subhead "Negro Entered Girl's Room and Then the Next World." The Columbia Herald in Tennessee headed it "Negro Lynched in Cracker State," whereas the Santa Fe New Mexican's front-page headline read "Georgia Adds Another Mark to Its Lynching Record."

Across all versions, the accusation and the reported confession were presented as fact, and Toler was identified only as "a negro," with no statement of the race of the girls or of the mob. Reprints continued in weeklies in South Carolina, Vermont, Missouri, Tennessee and Florida through August 19. No account from a Georgia newspaper or from the Black press was found for the weeks after the lynching.

accounts.gist: A girl woke when an intruder lifted the mosquito netting and screamed; a posse found Toler in a corn field the next afternoon, accused him, and he 'confessed'; at about 1 a.m. a mob of over 100 tied him to a tree, shot him and dispersed.

accounts.label: Associated Press version
accounts.gist: About one hundred men caught 'Tolera', tied him to a tree and shot him; the 'great excitement' abated once he was lynched.

accounts.label: Weekly digest rewrite
accounts.gist: A 'posse of infuriated citizens' found him 'pulling fodder' on a nearby plantation; questioned, he 'made a full confession' and was bound to a tree and shot.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Helena dispatch nearly verbatim, stating the accusation and the posse's claim of a confession as fact.
South Carolina weeklies headed it 'Promptly Lyncher Him' / 'Negro Entered Girl's Room and Then the Next World'; Pensacola's AP headline read 'Mob Made Quick Work of Him'.
The Santa Fe New Mexican headlined 'Georgia Adds Another Mark to Its Lynching Record', while still printing the confession claim as fact.

conflicts.note: Most versions, including the fullest text, give 1 a.m.; the 11 o'clock figure in A1 and the '4 o'clock' in A24 look like misprints of the same dispatch.
The condensed Western versions read 'seventy-seven'; the fuller text and the Florida digest say seven.

record_check.dossier: Not in official custody: a searching posse found him in a field, accused him, and he was killed early the next morning; no officers are mentioned.
No hanging: he was tied to a tree and shot to death; search, capture and shooting are supported.
Supported: early Thursday morning, August 11 (A1 says 11 a.m., A14 Wednesday night).
